title: The bicycle with no pedals
hook: The first bicycle had no pedals. Riders sat on it and kicked along the road.
peek: In 1817 Karl Drais rode a wooden two-wheeled machine out of Mannheim in Germany. It had a steerable front wheel but no pedals and no chain: the rider sat astride it and pushed along the ground with their feet, much like a child's balance bike.
lede: On 12 June 1817, Karl Drais, a forestry official in Mannheim, set off on a machine he called the Laufmaschine, or running machine. It had two wooden wheels in a line, a seat and handlebars that turned the front wheel. There were no pedals. Riders pushed off the ground with their feet and coasted, and Drais rode out to a coaching inn and back in about an hour, though accounts of the distance vary.

bullets.text: The big new idea was balance. By steering the front wheel, a rider could stay upright on two wheels in a line while gliding, something few people had imagined possible.

Some historians suggest the timing was no accident. After the 1815 Tambora eruption, the cold year of 1816 brought poor harvests and expensive horse feed, and a horseless way to travel looked appealing. Others doubt the link.

In 1819 the running machine became a fashion in London, where versions were called hobby horses or dandy horses. The craze faded fast, partly because riders took to smooth pavements and some cities banned them.
Pedals did not arrive for decades. In the 1860s French makers fixed cranks to the front wheel, and the chain-driven safety bicycle of the 1880s finally gave us the familiar shape.
Drais's design lives on in the pedal-free balance bikes that young children use to learn to ride. They learn to steer and balance first, just as his riders did.
